name: Shanghai
info: Shanghai is a city on the southern estuary of the Yangtze River in China, a fishing village and market town that became a treaty port in 1842, a commercial and financial hub, and a municipality of tens of millions.

facts.founded: The earliest Neolithic settlements known in the area belong to the Majiabang culture (5000 to 3300 BCE); Shanghai was made a market town in 1074 and the seat of a county in the early 1290s.
facts.where: On the southern estuary of the Yangtze River on China's east coast, on a flat alluvial plain bisected by the Huangpu River, bordering Zhejiang to the south and Jiangsu to the west and north.
facts.known: Qinglong Town and the cotton trade; the treaty port opened in 1842; the International Settlement and French Concession; the Bund; the founding of the Chinese Communist Party in 1921; the Battle of Shanghai in 1937; Pudong and Lujiazui
facts.today: Shanghai is a provincial-level municipality of China, divided into 16 districts, and the country's most populous city.

t: Shanghai began as a fishing village and a market town on the Huangpu River, rose with the cotton trade and the Qing customs office, and became one of five treaty ports after the First Opium War ended in 1842.

From 1843 foreign concessions grew beside the walled Chinese city, and in the 1920s and 1930s the city was a commercial and financial hub of the Asia-Pacific region, the birthplace of Chinese cinema and the place where the Chinese Communist Party was founded.
Japan invaded in 1932 and took the Chinese-held districts in 1937, the People's Liberation Army took the city in 1949, and economic reform from 1990 brought the development of Pudong.
dyk: The first Western atelier in Shanghai was established in 1864 inside the Tushanwan orphanage, and the city produced China's first fictional feature film, An Orphan Rescues His Grandfather, in 1923.
ev: Qinglong Town is established and becomes a major trading port
Shanghai becomes a county under Songjiang Prefecture
A city wall is built to protect the town from Japanese pirates
The Treaty of Nanking opens Shanghai as one of five treaty ports
The Chinese Communist Party is founded in the French Concession
The Battle of Shanghai ends in Japanese occupation of the Chinese-held districts
The People's Liberation Army takes control of the city
Deng Xiaoping permits economic reforms and Pudong is developed

sections.origins:
Shanghai stands on the southern estuary of the Yangtze River, on an alluvial plain formed by the river's deposits and by later land reclamation. The south flank of the Yangtze Delta began to develop after the maximum Holocene marine transgression, and as sediment built up new land, shell-rich sand ridges known as Gangshen formed in what are now the Jinshan and Fengxian districts. The earliest Neolithic settlements known in the area date to the Majiabang culture (5000 to 3300 BCE), overlapped by the Songze culture from about 3800 to 3300 BCE. At the Songze site in Qingpu District archaeologists found the prone skeleton of a man aged 25 to 30, one of the earliest known inhabitants. By the 4th century the shoreline had reached the Xinzhuang, Minhang and Nanqiao line, and the land east of it was fully formed before the Tang dynasty.

In the Spring and Autumn period the area belonged to the Kingdom of Wu, which Yue conquered and Chu in turn conquered. In the Warring States period it lay in the fief of Lord Chunshen of Chu, and local legends say he ordered the Huangpu River dug, which gave the city the nickname Shen. Fishermen made a fish tool called the hu, which named the outlet of Suzhou Creek and became the city's abbreviation. In 751 Huating County was established as the first county-level administration within modern Shanghai. The name Shanghai, written with the characters for 'upon' and 'sea', first appears in the 11th century, in the Song dynasty.
sections.growth:
The first great port of the area was not Shanghai but Qinglong Town in modern Qingpu District. Established in 746, it traded along the Yangtze and the Chinese coast and with Japan and Silla, and was later called a giant town of the Southeast. By 1077 the commercial tax collected there exceeded all the other taxes of the county combined. Siltation then narrowed the Wusong River and Qinglong declined, and the outer port of Huating County moved east to Shanghai Town on the developing Huangpu. Shanghai was raised from a village to a market town in 1074. Around the turn of the 14th century cotton growing and textile techniques, traditionally attributed to Huang Daopo, spread from Shanghai across the Yangtze Delta, and under the Ming cotton textiles were rapidly commercialised.

Two Qing policy changes made Shanghai one of the most important seaports of the delta. In 1684 the Kangxi Emperor reversed the prohibition on oceangoing vessels of 1525, and in 1732 the Qianlong Emperor moved the customs office for Jiangsu province from Songjiang to Shanghai. By 1735 it was the major trade port of the lower Yangtze, although it stood at the lowest level of the administrative hierarchy. By the mid-18th century wharves, warehouses, the customs house and guild halls had spread beyond the city walls. In the 1920s and 1930s the city was a commercial and financial hub of the Asia-Pacific region, and in 1936 it was one of the largest cities in the world, with 3 million inhabitants and about half of China's imports and exports.
sections.rulers:
The area belonged successively to the kingdoms of Wu, Yue and Chu and was part of Lord Chunshen's fief. Huating County was established in 751 by Zhao Juzhen, governor of Wu Commandery, and was governed under Suzhou and later Jiaxing. In 1277 Huating was raised to Songjiang Prefecture, and in the early 1290s five townships of eastern Huating were separated to form Shanghai County, with its seat at Shanghai Town. From the Yuan dynasty until 1927 central Shanghai was administered as a county under Songjiang Prefecture.

After the First Opium War, Britain, France and the United States established a presence outside the walled city, which remained under direct Chinese administration. The Shanghai Municipal Council was formed in 1854 to manage the foreign settlements, and in 1863 the British and American settlements joined as the Shanghai International Settlement, while the French kept their own concession. The council was wholly foreign-controlled, and no Chinese resident of the Settlement could join it until 1928. The Old City walls were pulled down in 1912.

On 7 July 1927 Shanghai was separated from Jiangsu and became a Chinese municipality under a mayor and council. Japan occupied the Chinese-held districts after 1937 and the foreign concessions from 8 December 1941, and held the whole city until its surrender in 1945. The concessions ended in 1943 for the British and Americans and in 1946 for the French. In 1949 the People's Liberation Army took control, and Shanghai was one of three municipalities not merged into neighbouring provinces.
sections.life:
Under the treaty system the city was divided between a more European western half and a more Chinese eastern half. Europeans and Americans called themselves Shanghailanders, and the Public Garden north of the Bund was for decades reserved for foreign nationals. The compradors, mediators for the foreign companies, formed a new class that mixed with local landlords into a Chinese bourgeoisie. Chinese society was organised in native place associations, guilds of traders from shared hometowns. White Russians who fled the Soviet Union in the 1920s and 1930s formed the second-largest foreign community, and about 30,000 Jewish refugees from Europe arrived in the 1930s.

Faiths and buildings reflected these arrivals. Buddhism had a presence from the Three Kingdoms period, when the Longhua and Jing'an temples were founded. The City God Temple was built in 1602, an honour usually reserved for prefectural capitals. The scholar Xu Guangqi was baptised by Matteo Ricci in 1603, and the Italian missionary Lazzaro Cattaneo brought Catholicism in 1608. Islam arrived in the Yuan dynasty, with Songjiang Mosque. The Bund took its early 20th-century form, and the city developed Art Deco buildings and shikumen houses of grey brick arranged in alleys called longtangs.

The vernacular is Shanghainese, a Northern Wu language. In the late 19th century it replaced Suzhounese as the prestige dialect of the Yangtze Delta. Shanghai was also the birthplace of Chinese cinema, with the short film The Difficult Couple in 1913 and the first fictional feature in 1923.
sections.crises:
In 1853 the Chinese-held Old City fell to the Small Swords Society, rebels linked to the Taiping Rebellion, and the Qing government regained it in February 1855. Between 1860 and 1862 Taiping forces twice attacked Shanghai and destroyed the eastern and southern suburbs but failed to take the city.

On 28 January 1932 Japanese forces invaded. More than 10,000 shops and hundreds of factories and public buildings were destroyed, Zhabei district was left in ruins, and about 18,000 civilians were killed, injured or declared missing. A ceasefire came on 5 May. The Battle of Shanghai in 1937 ended in the occupation of the Chinese-held districts. Under the occupation, people in the city experienced hunger, oppression or death. Japan placed Jewish refugees in the Shanghai Ghetto in Hongkou, where hunger and infectious diseases such as dysentery were common, and interned Britons, Americans and Dutch in camps, notably Lunghua, in 1943.

After the war inflation overwhelmed the city. In 1948 a price index rose from 2,199 in late November to 3,483 in early January 1949, then to 35,774 in early February and above 3,000,000 by April, and industrial output fell to 50 to 60 percent of its early 1948 level. Nationalist forces had vowed to make Shanghai a Stalingrad, but lost 153,000 of 210,000 defenders in the outer districts and did not hold the centre. In 1950 Nationalist air raids killed or injured many civilians, and the Cultural Revolution of 1966 to 1976 severely damaged the city's society.
sections.legacy:
Shanghai's modern history is closely tied to that of China. The Chinese Communist Party was founded in the French Concession in July 1921, and the May Thirtieth Movement of 1925, which began with the killing of a worker in a Japanese-owned cotton mill, led to strikes and nationwide protests. The Greater Shanghai Plan of the late 1920s laid out a new city centre in Jiangwan, outside the concessions.

The 1920s and 1930s left a row of neoclassical and Art Deco buildings on the Bund, among them the HSBC Building and Sassoon House, and Art Deco works by the architect László Hudec, who lived in the city from 1918 to 1947. The Old City kept traditional architecture such as the Yu Garden. Under the People's Republic the old racecourse was reclaimed in 1951 and its northern section became People's Park. In 1990 Deng Xiaoping permitted the city to begin economic reforms, which brought back foreign capital and developed Pudong and its financial district, Lujiazui.

Shanghai is today a provincial-level municipality divided into 16 districts, and the most populous city in China. The municipality has 24,874,500 people, of whom about 59.5 percent are registered locally, and about 40 percent come from other regions of China.

summary: Shanghai grew from a fishing village and cotton market on the Yangtze estuary into a treaty port after 1842, with foreign concessions beside the Chinese city. It was a commercial hub in the 1930s, was occupied by Japan, and was transformed again from 1990.
references: Michael Dillon, Shanghai: The Story of China's Most Dynamic City (Yale University Press, 2026)
Niv Horesh, Shanghai's Bund and Beyond (Yale University Press, 2009)
Linda Cooke Johnson, Shanghai: From Market Town to Treaty Port (Stanford University Press, 1995)
notes: START: the history article dates the earliest Neolithic settlements to the Majiabang culture (5000 to 3300 BCE); the main article says the western part was inhabited 6,000 years ago. I used -5000 with circa true. Shanghai as a town dates from 1074 (market town); county from early 1290s.

DISAGREEMENTS left out or hedged: city wall 1554 (main) vs 1553 (history), so given as 16th century; customs office moved to Shanghai in 1732 (main), the history article says the circuit was moved in 1730 (I used only 1732); 1932 world rank: the main article says fifth-largest city with 70,000 foreigners, the history says 3 million in 1936 with 35,000 to 50,000 Europeans (I used only the history figure for 1936); municipality: main says 7 July 1927 municipality, history says special city 1927 and municipality May 1930 (I wrote 'became a Chinese municipality' for 1927 as the main article does; the editor may prefer the history article's wording); PLA takeover day 27 May (main) vs 25 May (history), so only 1949 given; the Chinese Catholic arrival 1608 (Cattaneo, main) and the 1603 Ricci baptism of Xu Guangqi (history) are both given as they are not the same claim.

'Rise of 1735' and the 1684 reversal of the 1525 ban are from the main article. The history article says Shanghai County was set up in the early 1290s; the main article says 1292; the event label uses 1292.
Foreign settlements: the main article says a British settlement and an American one joined in 1863; the history article gives concession dates (1845, 1848, 1849) which I left out.

Concession end: Japan ended all concessions but the French after Pearl Harbor and the Anglo-Chinese treaty of 1943 conceded this (history); I wrote 1943 for the British and Americans and 1946 for the French. The editor should check that wording.

Population: 24,874,500 (2023) written as '24,874,500' without the year, per the guide; 59.5% hukou holders and 40.3% from other regions as the main article gives. 'most populous city' is the main article's claim.

Left out as the guide excludes them: economy and rankings, tourism, sports, airports, metro, universities, politics and the Shanghai Clique, climate, twin towns. Also left out for space: the 1988 hepatitis A epidemic, 2022 lockdown, the 1948 Gold Yuan reform, the Third Front, Green Gang and opium accounts, 1949 to 1952 campaigns, Cultural Revolution detail. The 'Shanghai Commune' section of the history article is empty.

The 1950 air raids: the article gives about 400 civilian casualties on 25 January and 1,448 reportedly on 6 February; I wrote only 'killed or injured many civilians' to avoid choosing a figure. 'Taiping rebels' attacking in 1860 to 1862 is from the main article; the Small Swords Society is called a Taiping-linked triad offshoot in the history article.
Name: the main article says the name's interpretation was disputed and gives conflicting accounts of its origin; I gave only the earliest occurrence in the 11th century.
